column2: The Lord speaks to Moses; the saying formula introduces instructions carried out publicly, not a change of addressee to Aaron.
The list distinguishes Aaron, his sons, his robes, oil, one calf, two rams and the basket. The singular possessive with robes remains his; no collective their is imposed.
The imperative calls the whole congregation to the tent entrance. Assembly language is retained without importing a later ecclesiastical institution.
Moses both obeys and gathers the congregation. The two clauses retain the explicit agent and the entrance location.
The word denotes what has been commanded to be done. The inherited passive English expresses the infinitive without inventing a new instruction.
Moses brings Aaron and his sons forward and washes them with water. No self-washing or immersion technique replaces the stated agency.

The sequence distinguishes tunic, belt, under-robe and shoulder-piece, followed by girding and fastening. Workmanship is retained for the construction phrase rather than replacing the Greek garment names with Hebrew terms.
Manifestation and Truth translate the Greek labels placed upon the oracle-piece. They are not silently replaced by transliterated Hebrew names.
The gold plate is on the front of the turban and is designated consecrated and holy. The inherited holy object supplies an English noun without adding an inscription here.
The incomplete clause continues into verse 11: Moses takes some anointing oil. No tent-anointing clause is inserted from a differently arranged text.
Seven sprinklings, altar and utensils, basin and stand, and then tent and contents all occur here. The final singular sanctification follows the tent; the repeated actions remain distinct.
Oil is poured on Aaron's head, followed by anointing and sanctification. These actions are not collapsed into a generic ordination statement.

The sons receive tunics, belts and headgear; they do not receive the singular high-priestly equipment listed for Aaron. Inherited turbans remains provisional alongside the earlier differing Greek headgear noun.
column3: Should the two headgear nouns receive distinct English labels after specialist garment review?

column2: Moses brings the calf, while Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head. The repeated designation for sin is retained rather than treating both actions as Moses' alone.

The slaughter subject is implicit; Moses is named at taking blood. Horns, finger, cleansing, base and consecration remain separate. Upon it preserves the atonement preposition without settling every ritual implication.
column3: Is atonement upon the altar or atonement concerning it the best contextual English?

column2: All inward fat, liver lobe, both kidneys and their fat are offered up. Both retains the emphatic paired organs; no additional animal part is supplied.
Calf, hide, flesh and dung are burned outside the camp. Burned up reflects the explicit burning verb, unlike the preceding offered up.
The ram is designated for a whole burnt offering; Aaron and his sons again lay hands on it. The shared subject is preserved despite the Greek singular verb with a compound subject.
Moses is explicitly named for both slaughter and pouring. The blood goes around the altar; repetition of Moses is source-supported.
Division is limb by limb; head, limbs and fat are then offered up. The inherited wording retains the anatomical ordering without describing an unstated cutting method.
Belly and feet are washed before the entire ram is offered. The two offering designations and sweet-savour description remain, with no ritual fire detail added to this verb.
This is explicitly the second ram, the ram of consecration. The hand-laying belongs to Aaron and his sons, not to a new unnamed group.
Right ear, right hand extremity and right foot extremity are named. The broad Greek extremity language is retained instead of supplying thumb and great toe from another base.
The same three right-side sites apply to Aaron's sons, followed by blood around the altar. Plural extremities and repeated Moses preserve the source's number and agency.
The list includes loin and right foreleg together with fats, liver lobe and kidneys. It is not harmonized to a fat-tail or hind-leg anatomical vocabulary.
One unleavened loaf, one oil loaf and one wafer are taken from the consecration basket. The Greek explicitly marks only the first loaf here as unleavened; no further adjective is inserted.
Everything is placed on Aaron's and his sons' hands and offered as a portion set apart. No specific waving movement is inferred from the offering noun.
Moses takes the items from their hands and offers them on the altar upon the consecration whole offering. The repeated agent and prepositional sequence remain visible.
The breast is removed as a presentation and becomes Moses' share. Presentation provisionally distinguishes epithema from the preceding aphairema without claiming a settled technical equivalence.
column3: What English term best distinguishes epithema in this ritual setting?

column2: Oil and altar blood are sprinkled on Aaron, his robes, his sons and their robes; the consecration list repeats all recipients. The repetition is meaningful and is retained.
Boiling and eating occur in the tent court, explicitly in a holy place. Flesh and basket loaves are both eaten by Aaron and his sons; no bread portion is omitted.
The remaining flesh and loaves are burned with fire. The passive does not name who burns them and applies to both kinds of remainder.
Seven days governs remaining at the entrance and consecration of their hands. The literal hands idiom is retained; the implicit he is not identified by an inserted name.
column3: Who is the understood subject of he shall consecrate, and should the hands idiom receive a clearer literary rendering?

column2: The doing today provides the pattern commanded for atonement on their behalf. The inherited he preserves the unstated agent rather than making a new divine speech claim.
Seven days, day and night, and the death-preventing purpose remain. Charges expresses the cognate guard/observance phrase without adding duties absent from the passage.
Aaron and his sons perform all the commanded words or matters. Things is idiomatic here and does not narrow the explicit all.
The eighth day follows the seven-day consecration. The council of elders translates gerousia and remains distinct from the whole congregation in verse 5.
Aaron is to take a calf for sin and a ram for a whole burnt offering, both unblemished. The plural adjective is retained in a position covering both animals.
The instructions go to the elders and specify one male goat, a calf and a year-old lamb. Year-old is singular beside lamb; the plural unblemished covers the latter offering pair.
Calf and ram are for deliverance, and flour is mixed with oil. Among you preserves the Greek en with the plural audience; today grounds the promised appearance.

The commanded items are brought before the tent, then the whole congregation approaches and stands before the Lord. Singular collective and plural verb are rendered naturally without dividing the congregation.
The command to do precedes the promised appearance of glory. The inherited among you retains the same locative expression as verse 4.
Aaron makes atonement for himself and his house before the people's gifts and atonement. House is the selected Greek reading, not silently replaced with people in the first clause.
Aaron approaches the altar and slaughters the calf for sin. His named agency prepares the contrast with his sons bringing blood next.
The sons bring blood to Aaron; he dips, applies it to horns and pours at the base. The English preserves the plural-to-singular transition.
Fat, kidneys and liver lobe are offered on the altar according to the command to Moses. The sin-offering description qualifies their animal, not an extra offering.
Flesh and hide are explicitly burned outside the camp. The repeated resumptive them in Greek is naturally represented by the two English objects.
The singular slaughterer and pourer remain distinct from the plural sons bringing blood. The whole burnt offering is not conflated with the preceding calf for sin.
They bring the offering by limbs, including the head; he places it on the altar. Parts makes the neuter pronoun readable without introducing organs beyond the source.
Belly and feet are washed in water and placed upon the whole burnt offering on the altar. Both successive upon phrases have a role and remain.
The initial presentation is plural, while taking and slaughter are singular. As the first refers back to the prior slaughter sequence; no additional atonement verb is supplied.
Prepared it as was fitting preserves the brief normative phrase. No detailed procedure is imported from parallel commands.
He fills his hands from the sacrifice and places it on the altar apart from the morning offering. The plural hands is retained rather than reduced to a single handful.
The calf and ram belong to the people's deliverance sacrifice. The sons bring blood and the singular priest pours it around the altar.
This extended object list continues into verse 20. Loin, covering fat, kidneys and their fat, and liver lobe remain distinct; punctuation helps the suspended construction.
He places fats on breasts, but they offer fats on the altar. The source shifts agency, and the inherited English correctly preserves that shift.
Aaron removes breast and right foreleg as a set-apart portion. The singular breast follows the plural breasts in verse 20 without a harmonizing correction.
Aaron raises hands over the people and blesses them, then descends after the offerings. Descent is not expanded into an architectural description.
Moses and Aaron enter together, emerge and bless all the people. Glory appears to all; both repeated all clauses are supported.
Divine fire consumes the offerings and fats, and the people are astonished and fall on their faces. The Greek reaction is not replaced by an added shout of joy.
Each son takes his own firepan; fire and incense precede presentation of strange fire. The negative says the Lord had not commanded it, without adding a specific alternative prohibition.
Fire comes from the Lord, consumes them, and they die before Him. The wording preserves both consumption and death rather than treating one as redundant.
God will be sanctified among those approaching and glorified in the congregation. Aaron is deeply stricken according to the Greek verb; silence is not substituted from a familiar version.
The sons of Uzziel are identified through Aaron's paternal uncle. Brethren expresses kinship broadly; holy things remains provisional for the plural holy expression.
column3: Does before the holy things or before the sanctuary best express the local plural ta hagia?

column2: The bodies are carried out in their tunics. The possessive is retained without asserting whose garments serve as the means of carrying.
column3: Does their refer to the dead priests' tunics or to the carriers' clothing?

column2: Removing headgear and tearing garments are forbidden to Aaron and his remaining sons. Israel is to mourn the burning; the Greek does not simply prescribe uncovered hair or dishevelment.
The entrance restriction is tied to avoiding death and the Lord's anointing oil upon them. The closing plural obedience clause includes the addressed survivors.
The Lord speaks directly to Aaron here. Moses is not inserted as intermediary from the more common introduction elsewhere.
The drink prohibition covers entering the tent and approaching the altar, with sons included. The repeated negative expresses avoidance of death; no diagnosis of the earlier sons' conduct is added.
Distinguishing holy from profane and unclean from clean explains the preceding instruction. The two paired distinctions remain separate rather than collapsed into moral purity.
The instruction verb is singular, addressing Aaron, while Israel is to learn all statutes through Moses. The by-the-hand idiom preserves mediation without physicalizing it.
Remaining sons take the remaining sacrifice and eat it unleavened beside the altar. Most holy represents the repeated holiness construction without losing the specified location.
The holy place and the prescribed portions for Aaron and sons are stated separately. The passive I have been commanded retains Moses' received authority.
The Greek says holy place and includes Aaron's house. Neither clean place nor daughters is substituted here from a different base; daughters are explicit in the following verse.
Foreleg and breast are brought with fat offerings; the enduring portion includes sons and daughters. The repeated separation language is retained without inventing a ritual gesture.
Diligently sought represents the emphatic paired seeking forms. The goat had already been burned; Moses' anger is directed to the two surviving sons.
Eating is connected with taking away the congregation's sin and making atonement. The source explicitly supplies to eat; the verbs are not reduced to an unexplained priestly entitlement.
No blood was brought into the holy place; the instruction includes the difficult front/inside phrase. The awkward inherited wording is held provisionally rather than silently guessing a location.
column3: How should kata prosopon eso be construed and punctuated in natural English?

column2: Aaron links today's offerings with what has befallen him. The final question introduced by me expects a negative response; a close alternative makes that expectation explicit while the literary question remains provisional.
column3: Would it not be unacceptable overstate the negative expectation, or should the literary question more clearly anticipate no?

column2: Moses hears and is pleased. The pronoun refers to Moses in the immediate narration; the verse does not claim a newly spoken divine ruling.
